title: Thanking your teachers
hookLine: the tradition owes honor to anyone who taught you even one letter
tomorrow: Rabbi Tarfon was in a hurry. so why say you needn't finish?

cards: A stack of thank-you cards on Noa's desk, most of them done. One is still blank: her drama teacher. Freshman year he put her in the chorus and told her she rushed every line.
She was furious for a month. He taught her exactly two things: slow down, and listen to the other actor. She's used both in every show since.

Does a teacher like that get a card? An old king had the same question, and his was much worse. David is walking up the Mount of Olives, weeping, barefoot, his head covered, running from his own son's revolt.
Then the news reaches him. His trusted counselor, Ahithophel, has gone over to the other side.

teach.h: ONLY TWO THINGS, FROM A TRAITOR.
teach.b: David prays that Ahithophel's advice will come to nothing, and in the story it does. You'd expect that to be the last word on the man. But Pirkei Avot remembers something else.
It says David learned only two things from Ahithophel, and still called him my teacher, my guide, my close friend, words the sages read in a psalm of David. Two things, from a man who betrayed him.
And from that the Mishnah draws a rule: whoever learns from another person a single chapter, a single law, a single verse, a single word, even a single letter, owes them honor. Even a single letter.
That's the detail to tell someone tonight: in this tradition, the honor isn't measured by how much you were taught, or by how kind the teacher was. It's owed for the letter itself.
So look back over these five years and you'll find teachers everywhere: parents, grandparents, a friend who explained a holiday, a sage dead for centuries, a stranger whose one sentence stuck.
Some taught you a whole book. Some taught you one letter. All of them count.

how: Jewish tradition honors teachers highly; Pirkei Avot teaches that anyone who taught you even a single letter is owed honor, and students traditionally thank and honor their teachers for life.

games.q: you're writing thank-you notes. a coach who was hard on you taught you one thing you still use. card or no card?
o: card: one thing is enough to owe thanks.
no card: thanks are for teachers who were kind.
no card: one thing isn't much of a lesson.
games.why: Avot: whoever teaches you even a single letter is owed honor. David honored a teacher of two things, who betrayed him.

practice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck, even one small thing, even someone it's complicated to thank. Write them a message now, on paper or on your phone: the one thing they taught you, and thank you.
Send it if you want to. Writing it is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Thanking your teachers: honor owed to anyone who taught you even one letter, the way David honored a teacher of two things.

carryVoice: Keep this: thank the teachers, even the ones who taught you one letter. Nine of fourteen.
